html:
The Luba Empire was a kingdom of the Upemba depression and the savanna of Katanga, in the south-east of what is now the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The map shows it from 1530 to 1900.

It grew from farming and fishing villages along the lakes of the upper Congo, where graves show rich chiefs from the 700s, part of the world of the Bantu peoples. Copper from Katanga was cast into crosses used as money.

Luba kingship was sacred. The king, the mulopwe, claimed a divine blood line through the founding hero Kalala Ilunga. A society of court historians, the Mbudye, kept the kingdom's history using lukasa memory boards, wooden boards studded with beads and shells that they "read" to recite lists of kings and places. Luba ideas of kingship spread to the Lunda and other neighbours.

The kingdom grew strongest in the 1700s and early 1800s, trading copper, salt, ivory and captives. Late in the 1800s it was weakened by succession wars and by raiders and traders such as Msiri and Tippu Tip. Its lands passed to the Congo Free State of King Leopold II, and later Belgian Congo.
